chapter_summary:
Parallel programming models provide the abstractions that programmers use to write parallel programs. The two main models are shared-memory and message-passing.

**Shared-memory programming:**

In a shared-memory model, all threads share a common address space. Communication occurs by reading and writing shared variables. This is the model used by OpenMP, POSIX threads (pthreads), and C++ threads.

Advantages:
- Simple programming model: threads communicate through shared variables.
- No explicit message passing: data is accessed directly.
- Good for fine-grained parallelism: threads can cooperate on small tasks.

Disadvantages:
- Synchronization is required to prevent race conditions.
- Cache coherence traffic can be high.
- Scalability is limited by the shared-memory bottleneck.

**Message-passing programming:**

In a message-passing model, each process has its own private address space. Communication occurs by sending and receiving messages. This is the model used by MPI (Message Passing Interface).

Advantages:
- Scalable to thousands of processes: no shared memory bottleneck.
- Explicit communication makes data movement visible to the programmer.
- Good for coarse-grained parallelism: processes work on large chunks of data.

Disadvantages:
- More complex programming model: explicit send/receive operations.
- Higher communication overhead for fine-grained tasks.
- Difficult to load balance.

**OpenMP:**

OpenMP is the standard API for shared-memory parallel programming. It uses compiler directives (pragmas) to specify parallel regions, loops, and synchronization.

Key directives:
- `#pragma omp parallel`: Creates a parallel region. Each thread executes the code inside the region.
- `#pragma omp for`: Distributes loop iterations across threads.
- `#pragma omp parallel for`: Combines parallel region and loop distribution.
- `#pragma omp critical`: Specifies a critical section (only one thread can execute at a time).
- `#pragma omp barrier`: Synchronizes all threads at a barrier.
- `#pragma omp reduction`: Combines partial results from all threads (e.g., sum, max).

**Fork-join model:**

OpenMP uses the fork-join model. The program starts with a single master thread. When a parallel region is encountered, the master thread forks (creates) a team of worker threads. At the end of the parallel region, the worker threads join (terminate) and the master thread continues.

**Performance analysis:**

For a parallel program with N threads and a fraction P of parallelizable work:
```
Speedup = 1 / ((1 - P) + P/N)
Efficiency = Speedup / N
```

For example, if P = 0.9 and N = 8:
```
Speedup = 1 / (0.1 + 0.1125) = 1 / 0.2125 = 4.7×
Efficiency = 4.7 / 8 = 59%
```

The efficiency is less than 100% because of the serial portion (1 - P) and parallel overhead (thread creation, synchronization, load imbalance).

**OpenMP scheduling:**
- **Static scheduling:** Loop iterations are divided evenly among threads. Good for uniform workloads.
- **Dynamic scheduling:** Loop iterations are assigned to threads as they become available. Good for non-uniform workloads.
- **Guided scheduling:** A hybrid that starts with large chunks and decreases the chunk size. Good for workloads with decreasing cost per iteration.

screens.title: Parallel Programming Models and OpenMP
screens.subtitle: Shared-memory vs message-passing, OpenMP directives, fork-join model, and performance analysis

narration.text: In this chapter we study the programming models programmers use to express parallel work and how OpenMP fits into shared-memory multicore systems. You will learn how threads share data in a common address space, why synchronization is necessary, and how message-passing contrasts with shared memory in scalability and explicit communication. We will also step through OpenMP primitives — parallel regions, loop distribution, critical sections, barriers, and reductions — and see how the fork-join model creates and destroys worker threads. Finally, we'll analyze performance with speedup and efficiency formulas and Amdahl's Law, and explore scheduling policies and common performance pitfalls such as false sharing. A concrete activity suggests parallelizing matrix multiplication, measuring run times for different matrix sizes and thread counts, and comparing static, dynamic, and guided schedules. By the end you should be able to choose an appropriate model, write basic OpenMP directives, and reason about where gains come from and why they are limited. Consider when shared-memory is simpler and when message-passing is necessary for scale: that question will guide practical design choices.

keyIdea.title: Why this chapter matters
keyIdea.text: Understanding programming models and OpenMP lets you write correct parallel code for multicore systems and reason quantitatively about expected speedups and limits.

screens.title: Shared-memory programming model
screens.subtitle: Threads share an address space and communicate via shared variables

narration.text: Shared-memory programming means multiple threads run inside the same process and access the same address space. Communication happens implicitly by reading and writing shared variables; there is no explicit send or receive step. This model is used by OpenMP and POSIX threads and is convenient for fine-grained cooperation because threads can directly update shared data structures. A concrete example is parallelizing a loop where each thread writes its partial result into an array slot; threads can read neighbors’ values without message-passing. However, shared memory requires care: without synchronization you can get race conditions where two threads update the same variable concurrently and the result depends on timing. Cache coherence protocols mask some complexity by keeping caches consistent, but they introduce traffic and latency. A common misconception is that shared-memory makes correctness trivial—it's often easier syntactically, but correctness requires explicit synchronization when data is shared. In practice you design data ownership or use synchronization primitives like locks, critical regions, or reductions to preserve correctness. Think about who owns each variable and whether updates must be atomic. That design helps limit unnecessary coherence traffic and prevents subtle bugs.

keyIdea.title: Shared-memory in brief
keyIdea.text: Threads share memory for direct communication; requires synchronization and attention to cache effects.

content.html:
Core Concept

Shared-memory programming model

Threads run in a single address space and communicate by reading and writing shared variables. This is the model used by OpenMP and pthreads.

Advantages
  • Simple access to shared data, no explicit messages.
  • Good for fine-grained cooperation and low-latency updates.
Disadvantages
  • Needs synchronization to prevent races.
  • Cache coherence traffic and limited scalability.
Concrete example
A parallel loop where each thread computes a partial sum and writes to an array slot. Threads can later reduce those slots into a final sum. Without synchronization, updating a shared accumulator can produce incorrect results due to races.
Key Takeaway

Shared memory is convenient but you must design ownership and synchronization to avoid races and minimize cache traffic.

Common mistake

Assuming reads and writes are automatically safe; small data races can be silent and produce subtle bugs.

screens.title: Message-passing programming model
screens.subtitle: Processes with private memory communicate explicitly by messages (MPI)

narration.text: The message-passing model gives each process its own private address space and requires explicit send and receive operations to move data. MPI is the canonical A P I for this model. Because communication is explicit, data movement is visible in the program structure and can be optimized at the cost of programming complexity. Message-passing tends to scale well to thousands of processes because there is no single shared-memory bottleneck, and it suits coarse-grained parallelism where processes work on large data partitions and exchange messages at defined synchronization points. A concrete example is a distributed matrix multiply where each process owns a block of the matrix and sends border rows to neighbors. This explicit exchange clarifies data dependencies but requires careful design for load balancing and communication latency. A typical misconception is that message-passing eliminates synchronization needs; in fact, you still need to coordinate sends and receives and manage deadlock risks. Use message-passing when available memory is distributed across nodes or when you need scalability beyond a single shared-memory machine. Message-passing programming model means private address spaces with explicit communication that scales to many processes but increases programming complexity.. In practical terms, processes with private memory communicate explicitly by messages (mpi). A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Message-passing in brief
keyIdea.text: Private address spaces with explicit communication that scales to many processes but increases programming complexity.

content.html:
Comparison

Message-passing model

Each process has private memory; communication is done explicitly by sending and receiving messages. MPI is the standard interface.

Advantages
  • Scales to thousands of processes without shared-memory bottlenecks.
  • Makes data movement explicit and visible to the programmer.
Disadvantages
  • More complex code due to explicit send/receive calls.
  • Higher overhead for fine-grained communication and load balancing.
Concrete example
A distributed matrix multiplication where processes own blocks and exchange boundary rows explicitly. Communication cost must be accounted for in performance calculations.
Key Takeaway

Message-passing makes data movement explicit and scales well, but requires careful design for latency and load balance.

Common misconception

Believing that message-passing removes all synchronization; sends and receives must still be coordinated to avoid deadlock.

screens.title: OpenMP fundamentals
screens.subtitle: Pragmas that create parallel regions, distribute loops, and manage reductions

narration.text: OpenMP is a shared-memory A P I that uses compiler directives—pragmas—to specify parallelism without rewriting the entire program. The most common directives are parallel, for, parallel for, critical, barrier, and reduction. The parallel directive marks a region where a team of threads executes the same code. The for directive distributes loop iterations among threads, often the simplest way to gain parallelism in compute-bound loops. Combined parallel for both creates the team and distributes the loop in one annotation. Critical declares a section where only one thread may execute at a time; it's useful to protect updates to shared data but can become a serial bottleneck. Barrier synchronizes threads until all reach the barrier. Reduction collects per-thread partial results into a single value using associative operations like sum or max. A typical example is summing an array: using a reduction avoids races and avoids a serial critical, giving both correctness and performance. A misconception is that adding pragmas always speeds up code—if the serial portion is large or synchronization overhead is high, pragmas may reduce performance. Use them where parallel work is abundant and independent.

keyIdea.title: OpenMP in practice
keyIdea.text: Use pragmas carefully: choose for/reduction for loop parallelism and avoid overusing critical sections to maintain speedup.

content.html:
Definition

OpenMP fundamentals

Compiler directives that mark parallel regions, split loops, and handle synchronization and reductions.

#pragma omp parallel
Creates a team of threads; each runs the region body.
#pragma omp for
Distributes loop iterations across threads.
critical / barrier / reduction
Synchronize access, wait for all threads, and combine partial results safely.
Example card
/* Parallel sum with reduction */
#pragma omp parallel for reduction(+:sum)
for (int i = 0; i < N; ++i) {
  sum += a[i];
}
Key Takeaway

Reductions are preferable to critical sections for associative combines because they avoid serializing updates.

screens.title: Fork-join execution model
screens.subtitle: Master thread forks workers at parallel regions and rejoins them after completion

narration.text: OpenMP follows the fork-join model: the program starts as a single master thread; when a parallel region is reached the master forks a team of worker threads that execute the region in parallel; at the end of the region the team joins and the master thread continues. This pattern is lightweight to express and maps well to many loop-parallel problems. A concrete example is a parallel for: the master encounters the annotated loop, creates threads, distributes iterations, waits for workers to finish, and then continues serially. Synchronization primitives such as barriers, critical sections, and reductions control visibility and ordering inside the parallel region. A common error is to assume threads persist across separate parallel regions—unless you use nested or persistent thread models, workers are typically created and destroyed at each region boundary which adds overhead. Another misconception is that fork-join hides the cost of thread creation; thread creation, scheduling and synchronization all contribute to parallel overhead and can reduce efficiency. Plan parallel regions to amortize creation costs over sufficient work, and prefer larger parallel regions that contain multiple loop constructs when appropriate.

keyIdea.title: Fork-join summary
keyIdea.text: Threads are created and destroyed around parallel regions; balance region granularity to amortize overhead.

content.html:
Process Flow

Fork-join execution model

  1. Start with a single master thread running serial code.
  2. Encounter a parallel region; master forks worker threads.
  3. All threads execute the region; use synchronization as needed.
  4. At region end, workers join and master resumes serial execution.
Pro tip
Group work into coarser parallel regions to reduce thread creation and synchronization overhead.
Concrete example
A function runs serially, then a parallel for is executed where the master creates N threads; after loop completion threads join and the function continues serially.
Common mistake
Placing many tiny parallel regions in hot code so thread management overhead dominates runtime.
Key Takeaway
Balance fork-join boundaries to amortize thread overhead and improve efficiency.

screens.title: OpenMP loop parallelism and reduction
screens.subtitle: A compact code example showing parallel for and reduction

narration.text: Let's walk through a small, concrete OpenMP example that sums an array using a parallel for with a reduction. The reduction clause tells the runtime to give each thread a private partial sum, then combine those partial sums safely at the end. This avoids the race and the overhead of a critical section. In the example code the pragma appears immediately above the loop; the compiler generates code to fork threads, distribute iterations, and perform the reduction. A key point: reductions require associative operations such as addition or max so partial results can be combined in any order. A misconception is to think reductions are only syntactic sugar; they also avoid synchronization bottlenecks by letting threads work independently and combining efficiently. As you test this on different thread counts, you'll see near-linear speedup for large N but diminishing returns as the serial fraction and overheads appear. When you can't use a reduction—say for a non-associative combine—design careful synchronization or redesign the algorithm to be associative. OpenMP loop parallelism and reduction means use reduction for associative combines to avoid racing and serial critical sections while enabling efficient parallel merges.. In practical terms, a compact code example showing parallel for and reduction. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Reduction pattern
keyIdea.text: Use reduction for associative combines to avoid racing and serial critical sections while enabling efficient parallel merges.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough

Parallel sum with reduction

int N = 1000000;
double sum = 0.0;
#pragma omp parallel for reduction(+:sum)
for (int i = 0; i < N; ++i) {
  sum += a[i];
}
This pattern gives each thread a private sum and merges them after the loop. It's both correct and efficient for associative operations.
Explanation
  • parallel for: creates threads and distributes iterations.
  • reduction(+:sum): private partial sums then combine safely.
  • Avoid critical sections for frequent updates; they serialize work.
Key Takeaway

Reductions are the preferred pattern for associative aggregation in OpenMP loops.

screens.title: OpenMP scheduling policies
screens.subtitle: Static, dynamic, and guided schedules for loop iteration assignment

narration.text: OpenMP offers different scheduling policies to distribute loop iterations among threads: static, dynamic, and guided. Static scheduling divides iterations evenly and assigns fixed chunks to threads; it works well when each iteration has similar cost and minimizes scheduling overhead. Dynamic scheduling gives threads chunks as they become free; it's useful when iteration costs vary because faster threads pick more work, improving load balance at the expense of higher scheduling overhead. Guided scheduling is a hybrid: it hands out large chunks initially and reduces chunk size over time; it's good when early iterations are heavy and later ones are lighter. A practical example is a loop where processing time depends on input size per iteration; static would load-balance poorly, dynamic would adapt but at higher runtime overhead, and guided can offer a middle ground. When measuring, try different chunk sizes—smaller chunks can improve balance but increase overhead. A misconception is to default to static scheduling because it's simple; while often fastest for uniform workloads, it can drastically underperform on imbalanced loops. Use measurement to select the appropriate policy and chunk size.

keyIdea.title: Scheduling rules
keyIdea.text: Choose static for uniform work, dynamic for irregular work, and guided to balance large-to-small workloads while reducing overhead.

content.html:
Comparison

OpenMP scheduling policies

Static
Evenly divides iterations; minimal overhead; best for uniform work.
Dynamic
Threads grab work as they finish; good for irregular work but higher overhead.
Guided
Starts with large chunks and reduces size; hybrid approach for many cases.
Concrete scenario
Processing a set of tasks where early tasks take much longer than later ones: guided scheduling hands large chunks first then smaller ones, reducing imbalance while keeping overhead moderate.
Pro tip
Experiment with chunk size. For dynamic and guided schedules, tune chunk size to trade off overhead and balance.
Key Takeaway
Select scheduling by workload variability and verify with measurements.

screens.title: Race conditions and synchronization
screens.subtitle: Why updates to shared variables must be protected

narration.text: A race condition occurs when two or more threads access the same memory location and at least one access is a write, and the final outcome depends on the relative timing. In shared-memory programs this commonly happens when threads update a shared accumulator or a shared data structure without protection. Synchronization primitives such as critical sections, locks, and barriers enforce ordering or exclusive access to avoid races. However, synchronization introduces overhead and can reduce parallel efficiency if overused. A common pattern to avoid frequent synchronization is to have each thread work on private data and then use a reduction or a single synchronized combine at the end. Another pitfall is believing that atomic operations are a cure-all; atomics are cheaper than full locks for simple updates, but they still serialize conflicting updates and can suffer from contention. When debugging races, look for non-deterministic failures and use tools or deliberate instrumentation. The design goal is to minimize synchronization points while ensuring correctness through ownership, privatization, or efficient aggregates like reductions. Race conditions and synchronization means protect shared writes with synchronization or use privatization and reductions to eliminate frequent contention.. In practical terms, why updates to shared variables must be protected. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Avoiding races
keyIdea.text: Protect shared writes with synchronization or use privatization and reductions to eliminate frequent contention.

content.html:
Definition

Race conditions and synchronization

Races happen when concurrent accesses to shared memory are not ordered and at least one is a write. Use synchronization to guarantee correctness.

Common strategies
  • Privatize per-thread data and reduce at the end.
  • Use reduction clauses or atomics for simple updates.
  • Use locks/critical for complex shared updates, but sparingly.
Concrete example
Multiple threads incrementing a shared counter without protection can lose increments. Use atomic increment or have each thread count locally then combine results.
Common mistake
Wrapping every update in a lock; excessive locking kills parallelism and creates contention.
Key Takeaway
Design for minimal necessary synchronization: privatize, reduce, or use targeted atomics when appropriate.

screens.title: Cache coherence and false sharing
screens.subtitle: How cache lines and placement of variables affect performance

narration.text: Cache coherence keeps multiple caches consistent when threads share memory, but this mechanism can generate traffic. False sharing happens when different threads modify distinct variables that happen to reside on the same cache line. Although threads are not logically sharing a variable, a write by one thread invalidates the cache line in other cores and forces reloads, causing unnecessary coherence traffic and performance loss. A typical example is two threads incrementing separate counters stored adjacently in an array; because the counters sit on the same 64-byte cache line, updates bounce the line between cores. The common fix is padding or aligning per-thread data so that variables used by different threads fall on separate cache lines. Another approach is to use per-thread arrays or structures and reduce them at a synchronization point. A misconception is to assume that data locality always helps; misaligned or tightly packed shared data can actually cause worse performance due to false sharing. When analyzing poor scaling, examine memory layout and measure cache-miss or coherence counters if available. Cache coherence and false sharing means place thread-private variables on separate cache lines or pad structures to prevent unnecessary coherence traffic and restore scalability.. In practical terms, how cache lines and placement of variables affect performance. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Avoid false sharing
keyIdea.text: Place thread-private variables on separate cache lines or pad structures to prevent unnecessary coherence traffic and restore scalability.

content.html:
Definition

Cache coherence & false sharing

False sharing occurs when threads modify different data in the same cache line, causing unnecessary invalidations and reduced performance.

Why it matters
Even logically independent updates can serialize due to hardware cache behavior, reducing speedup.
Concrete mitigation
Pad per-thread counters to 64 bytes or use per-thread arrays so that threads write to separate cache lines and avoid bouncing traffic.
Pro tip
When profiling shows poor scaling, test with padded data structures to confirm false sharing as the cause.

screens.title: OpenMP vs MPI trade-offs
screens.subtitle: When to prefer shared-memory approaches and when to use message-passing

narration.text: Deciding between OpenMP (shared-memory) and MPI (message-passing) depends on hardware, problem size, and complexity. OpenMP is simpler for multicore, single-node programs because threads share memory and pragmas can parallelize loops with minimal code changes. It works well when memory is abundant on a single machine and parallelism is fine-grained. MPI is the right choice for distributed-memory systems and large-scale clusters because it avoids shared-memory bottlenecks and can scale to thousands of processes. However, MPI requires explicit message design, which increases programming complexity and can lead to communication overhead for fine-grained tasks. Hybrid approaches combine OpenMP and MPI: use MPI between nodes and OpenMP inside a node to exploit both models' strengths. A common misconception is that one model is universally superior; instead, match the model to the platform and workload. For rapid prototyping on a multicore server, start with OpenMP; for cluster-wide jobs or when memory is partitioned across machines, prefer MPI or hybrid designs. OpenMP vs MPI trade-offs means use openmp for ease on single-node multicores and mpi for distributed-memory scaling; consider hybrid approaches for best of both worlds.. In practical terms, when to prefer shared-memory approaches and when to use message-passing. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Model selection
keyIdea.text: Use OpenMP for ease on single-node multicores and MPI for distributed-memory scaling; consider hybrid approaches for best of both worlds.

content.html:
Comparison

OpenMP vs MPI

OpenMP
Shared-memory, easier to use for loops, good for multicore nodes.
MPI
Message-passing for distributed memory, scales to many nodes but requires explicit communication.
Concrete guideline
If your workload runs on a single shared-memory server, prefer OpenMP for simplicity. For cluster-scale jobs or when memory is partitioned across machines, use MPI or a hybrid MPI+OpenMP approach.
Key Takeaway
Select the model that matches hardware and workload; hybrid models often give the best resource use at scale.

screens.title: Activity: Parallel matrix multiplication with OpenMP
screens.subtitle: Guided steps to parallelize and measure speedup and scheduling effects

narration.text: The hands-on activity is to parallelize matrix multiplication using OpenMP, measure execution times, and compute speedup and efficiency. The recommended approach is to parallelize the outermost loop with a parallel for pragma so each thread computes independent rows or blocks. For each matrix size N = 512, 1024, 2048, run with 1, 2, 4, and 8 threads and record wall-clock times. Compute speedup using Speedup = 1 / ((1 - P) + P/N) only when P is known; more directly compute measured speedup as T1 / TN and efficiency as speedup divided by thread count. Experiment with schedule(static), schedule(dynamic, chunk), and schedule(guided) to see how load balance and overhead trade off. To examine false sharing, observe runtime differences when per-thread temporary buffers are padded to separate cache lines. If you cannot run the code, describe expected outcomes: static scheduling should be best for uniform costs; dynamic helps imbalanced iteration costs; guided is a compromise. When plotting results, use speedup vs thread count curves to identify diminishing returns and compare against Amdahl's Law predictions. Activity: Parallel matrix multiplication with OpenMP means parallelize the outer loop, measure times across sizes and threads, evaluate scheduling effects and cache behavior to explain scaling results.. In practical terms, guided steps to parallelize and measure speedup and scheduling effects. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Activity outcome
keyIdea.text: Parallelize the outer loop, measure times across sizes and threads, evaluate scheduling effects and cache behavior to explain scaling results.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity

Matrix multiplication with OpenMP

Parallelize the outer loop using #pragma omp parallel for and test with N = 512, 1024, 2048. Measure for 1, 2, 4, 8 threads and compute speedup and efficiency.
/* Outer-loop parallelization sketch */
#pragma omp parallel for schedule(static)
for (int i = 0; i < N; ++i) {
  for (int j = 0; j < N; ++j) {
    double sum = 0.0;
    for (int k = 0; k < N; ++k) sum += A[i][k] * B[k][j];
    C[i][j] = sum;
  }
}
Measurement checklist
  • Record wall-clock times for each configuration.
  • Compute speedup = T1 / TN and efficiency = speedup / N.
  • Compare schedules and try padding to detect false sharing.
Key Takeaway
Empirical measurement is essential: theory guides expectations, experiments reveal real bottlenecks like coherence or imbalance.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.subtitle: Essential points to remember about models, OpenMP, and fork-join

narration.text: Let's summarize the most important ideas so you can recall them quickly. Shared-memory programs use threads that share address space and require synchronization to avoid races; OpenMP provides pragmas to express this parallelism. Message-passing programs use private address spaces and explicit sends and receives, and are better suited for large-scale distributed systems. OpenMP's fork-join model creates a team of threads at parallel regions and rejoins them afterward, so plan region granularity to reduce overhead. Use reductions instead of frequent critical sections for associative combines, and choose scheduling policies—static, dynamic, or guided—based on workload uniformity and overhead trade-offs. These core concepts determine correctness, scalability, and performance. Keep them in mind as you write or analyze parallel programs: the programming model constrains your options and shapes the optimizations you can apply. In practical terms, essential points to remember about models, openmp, and fork-join. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Key Concepts — Part 1

A compact collection of three essential ideas.

Shared-memory
Threads share an address space; synchronization prevents races but can limit scalability.
OpenMP directives
Use parallel, for, reduction, critical, and barrier to express parallel regions and synchronize safely.
Fork-join
Master forks workers at parallel regions and rejoins them at the end; region granularity matters for overhead.
Summary Takeaway

Use the shared-memory model and OpenMP for convenient multicore parallelism, but plan synchronization and region sizes to preserve correctness and performance.

screens.subtitle: Performance, scheduling, and pitfalls to watch

narration.text: Now remember the key performance formulas and pitfalls. Speedup equals one over the serial fraction plus the parallel fraction divided by threads; efficiency is speedup divided by thread count. Amdahl's Law shows that a serial portion limits maximum speedup even if the parallel fraction is large. Scheduling policy affects load balance and overhead: static for uniform work, dynamic for irregular work, and guided as a hybrid. Watch out for false sharing, where unrelated variables share a cache line and cause extra coherence traffic, and for overuse of critical sections that serialize execution. When optimizing, measure first: compare measured speedup curves to Amdahl's predictions, try different schedules, and check for cache-related performance drops. The combination of correct synchronization, proper scheduling, and careful data layout is what translates parallelism into real speedup on multicore systems.

keyIdea.title: Performance checklist
keyIdea.text: Calculate speedup and efficiency, apply Amdahl's Law, choose scheduling appropriately, and avoid false sharing and excessive synchronization.

Key Concepts — Part 2

Performance formulas and common pitfalls in parallel programs.

Speedup & Efficiency
Speedup = 1 / ((1-P) + P/N). Efficiency = speedup / N. Use these to set realistic expectations.
Amdahl's Law
A serial fraction limits maximum speedup even with infinite threads; quantify it to set goals.
Pitfalls
False sharing and excessive synchronization often explain poor scaling; adjust layout and sync points to fix them.
Final takeaway

Measure, reason with formulas, and apply model-specific patterns to turn parallel code into real performance gains.
